title: About This Channel
principle: Treat outside advice as a boost to your own judgment
why: He says the foundation is the viewer's own experience, skill and way of thinking; his videos only give a little extra boost, and your mileage may vary.
how: Use design lessons to sharpen judgment built by making and playing games, rather than as rules to follow blindly.
quote: The foundation is the viewer's experience, skill, and way of thinking.

title: Game Development Isn't a Game
principle: Treat paid game development as a job, not a hobby
why: Once money, sales and numbers are involved, development is a job like any other; indie developers become professionals too, and being a pro means being light on your feet and responding to demand.
how: Do assigned work well even when it isn't to your taste, and look for what makes it interesting and rewarding.
anti_pattern: Only working on what you personally enjoy once you're paid.
example: An artist who loves cute things texturing lifelike zombies and roaches.
quote: The job of a game developer is to create games, but the work itself is not a game.

title: Game Development Isn't a Game
principle: Design to the assignment's genre and goal, not your own taste
why: He made Kirby's Dream Land for newcomers despite being an experienced gamer and Meteos despite not being good at block puzzles; once you understand what makes games fun, you can create any kind of experience.
how: Write down the genre, goal and audience each project must fit, then find the fun within that brief.
anti_pattern: Designing games for yourself.
example: Kirby's Dream Land; Meteos.
quote: I view every project that comes my way as an assignment in which I create a game to fit a certain genre or goal.

title: Game Development Isn't a Game
principle: When you lose your way, return to entertaining players
why: Every developer shares one goal, entertaining players, and that desire supplies the motivation to keep going through development's challenges.
how: When stuck or demotivated, ask how the decision in front of you entertains the player and choose accordingly.
quote: If you feel like you've lost your way, just remember: entertain players.

title: Squeeze and Release
principle: Ask why other games do something before copying it
why: Reexamining why other games do things, instead of mimicking them, boosts your chances of making something fresh and innovative.
how: Before borrowing a mechanic, write down why it works in its source game and whether that reason applies to yours.
anti_pattern: Mimicking other games' features without understanding them.
quote: Don't just mimic the things other games are doing. Reexamine why they do them, and you'll boost your chances of making something fresh and innovative.

title: Game Awards
principle: Judge each game against its own goals and audience
why: Every game has its own values, goals and audience, and diversity is what makes games great, so one style isn't necessarily better than the next.
how: When evaluating a game, ask whether it achieves what it set out to do for its intended players instead of ranking it on one scale.
anti_pattern: Choosing one universal 'best' game.
quote: Every game has its own values, goals, and audience, so the idea of choosing one "best" game isn't something I can really get behind.

title: Game Awards
principle: Recognize ingenuity, not just commercial success
why: User-vote awards favor games that sold well; directors who know the struggle of making unique games can put ingenuity front and center, which creates possibilities.
how: When judging or recognizing work, include an originality criterion assessed by experienced creators alongside popularity.
anti_pattern: Equating sales or popularity with merit.
example: Japan Game Awards' Game Designers Award, voted by directors of unique games.
quote: For the Game Designers Award, ingenuity—not commercial success— is put front and center by directors who know the struggle of creating unique games.

title: Try Telling That to the Player
principle: When a compromise would hurt players, look for other solutions
why: Issues, varied tastes and technical limits are unavoidable, but you're making the game for the player and nobody else; developers are players too and should know how customers feel.
how: Before accepting a player-unfriendly compromise, search for alternative solutions.
anti_pattern: Expecting players to forgive problems caused by hard development.
quote: But when push comes to shove, you're doing this for the player, and nobody else.

title: Exercise While You Game!
principle: Pair play sessions with sustained aerobic exercise, like an exercise bike.
why: Playing takes your mind off the effort, so long sessions that would be tough breeze by, and aerobic exercise works best when sustained; he has pedaled for two hours.
how: Set up an exercise bike, stepper or treadmill in front of the screen and pedal through play sessions; racing games work well when pedaling feels like going faster.
anti_pattern: Pairing it with stealth games, where you unconsciously pedal slower.
example: Sakurai's own exercise-bike gaming sessions of up to two hours.
quote: But pedaling while you play a game helps take your mind off all that.

title: Exercise While You Game!
principle: Exercise at least a little regularly, even if you dislike it.
why: People who exercise tend to be far more productive than people who don't.
how: Build small home routines, such as adjustable dumbbells, when you can't get to a gym, and increase the load gradually.
anti_pattern: Going overboard; he hurt his legs climbing around 500 stairs.
quote: So it's better to exercise at least a little.

title: The Price of Games
principle: Support the creators of games you want by buying or subscribing.
why: Games need large teams plus marketing and release costs, yet prices have stayed flat, and a game's price means little if nobody plays it.
how: Buy the game, or play it through a subscription, instead of hesitating.
quote: At the end of the day, the price of a game doesn't mean much if nobody plays it.

title: Making a Living Making Games
principle: Make and finish your own game to break into the industry.
why: It's the quickest, if not only, way in: you see which problems arise and how to solve them, and even designers need to think like programmers.
how: Pick any tool (Unity, Unreal Engine, JavaScript, Maker software) and start small; mimicking an existing game is fine at first.
quote: For starters, just take a shot at making your own game.

title: Making a Living Making Games
principle: Get people to play your game and act on their feedback.
why: Players' reactions show what to improve or what to carry into the next project, and distributing a game can also teach PR.
how: Ask friends, distribute it free online, or sell it if confident; then revise the game or apply the lessons next time.
quote: And once people play your game, find out what they think— and either go back and make improvements, or carry that experience and knowledge into your next project.

title: Making a Living Making Games
principle: Show originality in the game you submit with applications.
why: Many people want to make games; companies want people who can make fun games, and an imitative idea won't help your case.
how: Send a game with an original idea along with your application, even if you don't meet every listed requirement.
anti_pattern: Submitting an imitative game idea.
quote: That said, an imitative game idea won't do much to help your case. Find a way to let your originality shine.

title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
principle: Make the extra effort that sets your work apart.
why: Most creative works have to do what they can to stand out from the crowd, even when the labor is immense.
how: Identify the touches that will make your game feel extra special, like orchestral music or a CG movie, and commit to them.
example: Melee's orchestral arrangements and first CG movie.
quote: Still, I'd say most creative works— not just games— have to do what they can to set themselves apart from the crowd.

title: That Was Then, This Is Now
principle: Keep playing new games instead of judging by nostalgic standards.
why: Works from our youth leave deep imprints, and it's a shame to bounce off modern games just because they can't match those memories.
how: Regularly try new titles and expand beyond what you already like.
anti_pattern: Treating old games as the standard all others are held to.
quote: It's better to keep trying new things, right?

title: Prep Your Proposals Hot and Fast
principle: Write proposals quickly while your motivation is hot
why: Nothing good comes from dragging things out; momentum matters, and the longer a proposal sits, the less fresh it becomes.
how: Prepare first by sorting ideas into main topics and subtopics; once the outline and main points are itemized, go straight into the presentation in one push.
anti_pattern: Droning on, or letting the draft sit.
quote: The longer you let it sit, the less fresh it'll be.

title: Prep Your Proposals Hot and Fast
principle: Treat a rejected proposal as your failure to show its appeal
why: The proposal must make funders and talent think "We should definitely do this"; showing the appeal is the presenter's job.
how: When a proposal is turned down, rework how it demonstrates the fun instead of blaming the reviewers.
anti_pattern: Convincing yourself the other party doesn't have taste.
quote: It's your responsibility as the presenter to show off your game's appeal.

title: Sora Ltd.
principle: Keep management overhead from crowding out creative work
why: Creators who go independent and hire a team often get bogged down in the management needed to keep employees paid, leaving no time for the game itself.
how: Before building a studio, weigh the management load; Sakurai instead stays a one-person contracting company, directs on-site at partner studios, and focuses on one project at a time.
anti_pattern: Forming a company and hiring staff by default, then losing creative time to running it.
example: Sora Ltd.
quote: leaving no time to focus on what matters most: creating their game.

title: Sora Ltd.
principle: Share a publisher's risk by tying your pay to sales
why: The publisher sees no profit until the game is on sale, so taking no fee during development shares that risk with them, though it is a high-risk arrangement.
how: Consider contracts that pay from sales after release instead of a monthly fee, but only if you can absorb earning nothing should the project fall through.
example: Sakurai's Sora Ltd. contracts
quote: I don't ask for compensation during the project as a way of sharing that risk with them.

title: You'll Forget the Hardship, But the Game Will Endure!
principle: Avoid compromises you'll regret once the game ships
why: You forget the difficulties of a project, but the parts you got wrong stay in the game; Sakurai still remembers a mistake in Kirby's Adventure's ending.
how: When tempted to take the easy way out, weigh the effort against a flaw that will be permanent.
anti_pattern: Taking the easy way out and making too many compromises.
example: Kirby's Adventure ending: the screen shakes when it should have flashed white
quote: You'll forget the hardship, but the game will endure!

title: You'll Forget the Hardship, But the Game Will Endure!
principle: Weigh your effort against how many players will feel the result
why: If 1,000 people play your game, the impact is 1,000 times your hardship; big audiences sweep the hardship away.
how: Remember that actual people will buy the game, and apply yourself for them.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: over 29 million copies, about Australia's population
quote: If 1,000 people play your game, the resulting impact is 1,000 times greater than your hardship.

title: You'll Forget the Hardship, But the Game Will Endure!
principle: Work efficiently first, then do everything you can for customers
why: Sakurai isn't saying workers should go through needless hardship; effort should go into serving players, not into waste.
how: Set up an efficient workflow, then put full effort into what players will experience.
anti_pattern: Needless hardship.
quote: But once we're set up to work efficiently, we should do everything we can to serve our customers.

title: Directors Need to Be Unique
principle: Train yourself to notice details and perspectives others miss
why: The one trait good directors share is a keen sensibility that latches onto tiny details and sees things differently from other people.
how: When reviewing builds or other games, write down the small details in visuals, game essence, animation and story that most people would overlook.
anti_pattern: Assuming there is one standard way to be a director.
quote: If you show them something, or run an idea by them, they're the kind of people who'll latch onto tiny details, and perceive things that most others would miss.

title: Directors Need to Be Unique
principle: Turn your personal thoughts and feelings into what distinguishes your game
why: Directors use their own thoughts and feelings to set their games apart; the role, like a game, needs a touch only that person can give.
how: For each major decision, state your personal take and how it differs from the genre's default, and keep it deliberately.
quote: A director position—just like a game itself— calls for a personal, unique touch that only that person is capable of offering.

title: Games and Eye Strain
principle: Fix your work environment first to reduce eye strain
why: Brightness, blue-light glasses, eyedrops and supplements help, but nothing is as effective as changing the work environment.
how: If your monitor is under 60 cm away, move it back toward at least one meter and use a larger monitor to compensate.
anti_pattern: Long sessions with screens close to your eyes.
example: He had severe eye strain and dry eyes during Smash Bros. Ultimate's development.
quote: There are plenty of methods out there, but I'd say nothing is as effective as changing your work environment.

title: Games and Eye Strain
principle: Match screen brightness to your surroundings
why: Lowering brightness to match the room is one of several ways to reduce eye strain.
how: Adjust monitor brightness to the room's lighting, and add glasses or eyedrops as secondary measures.
quote: You can lower screen brightness to better match your surroundings.

title: Just Do It Already!
principle: Start the task now instead of waiting for motivation
why: There's no point in overthinking when unmotivated; motivation comes later, once your hands are moving.
how: Take the first physical step at once: open the document and write a line, or open the canvas and draw.
anti_pattern: Waiting to feel motivated before starting.
quote: If you're feeling unmotivated, there's no point in overthinking it. The time is now. Get those hands moving.

title: Just Do It Already!
principle: Cut off distractions and keep a steady output
why: Social media, video sites, the internet and games are tempting, and you won't succeed without steady output.
how: Close distracting apps before each work block and produce something every day; save planning tricks for after you've started.
anti_pattern: Overthinking what the work means before doing it.
quote: You won't succeed without steady output.

title: Mastering Up
principle: Approach other developers' games with gratitude
why: Many other developers go through the same struggles to finish their games.
how: When playing or critiquing others' games, keep in mind the cuts and hardships behind them.
quote: I know that pain all too well, so I try to approach the games I play with gratitude.

title: How I Stuck With My Column
principle: Approach routine work loosely, not out of obligation
why: Working out of obligation or "for the sake of the industry" takes a major toll; staying looser let him keep a column going for 18 years and 9 months.
how: Shrug off pressure and duty, and put out what you think is good without overthinking it.
anti_pattern: Writing because you have to or because many people are reading.
example: Weekly Famitsu column: 640 articles.
quote: You have to enjoy it, not feel beholden to it.

title: How I Stuck With My Column
principle: Keep recurring deliverables small in time investment
why: He typically finished each column in about an hour, a reasonable investment that stayed sustainable even through busy dev periods and all-nighters.
how: Time-box recurring output to a short, fixed slot.
example: Weekly Famitsu column.
quote: When writing the columns, I typically finished in about an hour.

title: How I Stuck With My Column
principle: Choose recurring output that uses strengths you already exercise
why: As a director, conveying ideas isn't a chore for him, it's what he does, so writing a column came naturally.
how: Pick side projects that line up with the skills your main job already trains.
quote: Being a director, I don't find conveying ideas to be too much of a chore.

title: ♪ PRESS START
principle: Fix a recurring project's run length and per-edition scope upfront
why: Sakurai planned PRESS START for ten years from the start and saw it through; researching more songs than each program used would have been too much during game development.
how: Before launching, decide the total run and the size of each edition (PRESS START: 14-16 program pieces, about 60 songs) so it fits beside your main work.
anti_pattern: Open-ended side projects that grow until they compete with development.
example: PRESS START, ten annual concerts, nearly all full houses.

title: Family BASIC
principle: Start by sitting down and making a game with available tools
why: Family BASIC, bought with six months of allowance, is what showed Sakurai he could make games; without it there would be no Kirby or Smash Bros.
how: Pick whatever tool is accessible now and finish something small instead of waiting for better equipment.
anti_pattern: Waiting for ideal hardware or tools before starting.
example: Family BASIC on the Famicom.
quote: But the most important thing to do is to first sit down and try to make a game.

title: Games During My Childhood
principle: Remember your game may shape a child's lifelong tastes
why: The things we love as kids, and the joy they bring, strongly shape our adult tastes, and creators may have that effect on today's children.
how: Keep young players in mind as an audience whose experience with your game may stay with them for life.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate as the top game in CoroCoro Comic's 2019 survey.
quote: I'd say that the things we love as kids and the joy those things bring us go on to have a huge impact on our tastes in adulthood.

title: Broad Input, Broad Output
principle: Play many current games and finish them to know the bar
why: Sakurai needs to grasp the scope of modern games so what he delivers can be on par; he calls it a must.
how: Play as many different games as you can rather than one at length, and try to reach each ending.
anti_pattern: Sinking all your play time into a single title.

title: Broad Input, Broad Output
principle: Make regular output a long-term habit
why: Sakurai pairs input with habitual output (an 18-year-9-month Famitsu column, a daily team report, a daily screenshot, this channel); staying active with both, he says, lets you achieve great things.
how: Commit to a recurring output such as a weekly column or daily team report, and keep it going.
example: Weekly Famitsu column; Daily Report; Screenshot of the Day.
quote: Take a lot in, put a lot out. Stay active with both, and I think you can achieve great things.

title: Broad Input, Broad Output
principle: Reflect actively on whatever media you consume
why: Watching something can be very impactful if you reflect on its facets while you do; input you don't think about is wasted.
how: Choose the input form that suits you and note what works and why while playing or watching.
anti_pattern: Letting media go in one ear and out the other.
quote: make sure the media you consume doesn't go in one ear and out the other.

title: Unifying Visual Style
principle: Expect every artist to match the set style outside their specialty
why: Team members must produce the same visual style, so specialists sometimes make art outside their strengths; most artists are very good at matching a set style, and competition demands it.
how: Practice working in styles beyond your favorite, and budget for unification, which costs more as visual fidelity rises.

title: The Team Behind Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Commit fully: clear other work when a project needs all of you
why: Making a Smash Bros. would require all of Sakurai's time, so he turned down his other projects except one already in progress.
how: Before accepting a demanding lead role, decline or finish competing commitments instead of splitting your focus.
anti_pattern: Taking a project that needs everything while juggling other agreements.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl; only Mushiking was kept.
quote: There I was with a task only I could do, and people were looking to me to do it.

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games Introduction Video
principle: Study improving games and generating new ideas as learnable skills
why: Sakurai frames how to make games better and how to come up with new ideas as topics that can be taught, and calls teaching them his ultimate goal for the channel.
how: Treat improving an existing design and generating new ideas as two distinct skills to study and practice deliberately.
quote: If you're wondering how to make games better or how to come up with new ideas, I delve into those topics on this very channel.

title: Keep Your Internal Pressure High
principle: Keep a proposal to yourself until the first draft is finished
why: Discussing ideas makes you feel fulfilled and releases the internal pressure that gives a proposal its force. A document written without sharing a word burns hotter than a compiled brainstorm.
how: Whenever you want to talk about the idea, write it into the document instead. Consult colleagues for weak points only once the draft is done.
anti_pattern: Talking an idea through before it's written, or substituting a group brainstorm for your own draft.
example: Sakurai's balloon and pressure-cooker metaphors.
quote: In other words, by releasing pressure, the ideas in your mind lose their power.

title: Keep Your Internal Pressure High
principle: Don't post ideas or progress on social media while creating
why: Posting ideas or progress vents the same pressure that should go into the work.
how: Hold back social media updates about a project while it's taking shape and put that energy into the work.
anti_pattern: Sharing work-in-progress for the instant satisfaction of reactions.
quote: Posting your ideas or progress on social media will vent your pressure—which you don't want.

title: Keep Your Internal Pressure High
principle: Picture how people will react to fuel the work
why: Imagining how your pitch audience and later your players will react, and which parts they'll love, gives you the strength to push on.
how: While writing and developing, picture specific reactions to specific parts of the game and use them as motivation.

title: Show and Tell: Some Rare Belongings
principle: Submit game proposals to open calls even before entering the industry
why: Sakurai's late-1980s entry to a Sega proposal promotion won him Associate Planner Certificate No. 004 and a visit to Sega before he had entered the industry.
how: Enter publisher or studio proposal contests and open calls with a concrete mechanic idea.
example: Sega Associate Planner Certificate No. 004, for a proposal like an action-focused Active Time Battle system.
quote: In the late 1980s, Sega had a promotion where people could submit game proposals— which is where I won this.

title: Special Crossover! #1
principle: Study your genre's foundational games firsthand
why: You can't talk about gaming history without arcade games. Playing them shows how clever ideas like horizontal scrolling, separate bomb buttons, fuel gauges, jumping and parallax built on each other.
how: Play the early titles in your genre and note which mechanic each introduced.
example: Scramble's groundwork for side-scrollers like Gradius. Donkey Kong's jumping. Moon Patrol's parallax scrolling.
quote: But you just can't talk about gaming history without including arcade games in the mix, I'd say.

title: Making Games as Part of a Company
principle: Treat cooperation at work as a choice you made, not a burden
why: Friction between positions is inevitable, but company work is about supporting and being supported; it's the path you chose, so cooperating serves everyone better than feeling forced.
how: When friction arises between roles, ask what you can do to help the other side do their best, and act on it.
anti_pattern: Thinking you're being forced into your job.
quote: Everyone at a company is in the same boat. Work together, and do what you can to bring out the best in each other.

title: Making Games as Part of a Company
principle: Follow the partner company's rules when you work within it
why: Sakurai is a freelancer, yet because much of his work involves cooperating with other companies, he does what's expected and always abides by their rules.
how: When joining or contracting with a studio, learn its rules and processes and follow them.
example: Sakurai's own freelance work with partner companies
quote: Still, much of the work I do involves cooperating with other companies, so I do what's expected of me and always abide by their rules.

title: Making Sequels
principle: Give every assignment your best, sequel or original
why: Sakurai sees meaning and value in both sequels and new titles; which he makes depends on who offers the work, and a sequel won't sell if it isn't well made.
how: Treat a sequel assignment with the same full effort as an original, because the quality of each entry drives sales of the next.
anti_pattern: Coasting on a series' name.
quote: What matters most is that I carry out my assignments to the best of my ability.

title: The Power of Suggestion
principle: Give yourself something to run from, not just a goal to reach
why: Sakurai went from last to first in foot races by imagining a three-meter machine chasing him; a deadline or endpoint closing in can be surprisingly effective motivation.
how: Frame upcoming milestones as something approaching that you must get ahead of.
anti_pattern: Running as if chasing your own shadow.
example: Sakurai's middle-school foot races
quote: instead of setting a target or a destination you're heading toward, give yourself something to run from.

title: The Power of Suggestion
principle: Tell yourself a task has only a few hours left
why: Thinking you can finish whenever lets work drift, while believing time is short gets things done; but it doesn't mean actually waiting for the last day.
how: Set a short, self-imposed time limit before starting each task, well ahead of the real deadline.
anti_pattern: Leaving work until the real last day, like summer homework.
quote: I believe you'll really get things done if you tell yourself you only have a few hours left.

title: Creators Change, Too
principle: Don't write off creators who leave the industry
why: Many who disappear go on to succeed elsewhere, securing lucrative patents or making groundbreaking advances in unrelated fields.
how: When a creator drops out of view, assume they may be doing fulfilling work somewhere else rather than calling them finished.
anti_pattern: Labeling vanished creators as washed up or finished.
example: Former colleagues who secured patents or made advances outside games.
quote: please don't write them off as “washed up” or “finished”!

title: Creators Change, Too
principle: Let yourself start something new as your experience grows
why: Staying put for a whole career is less common than moving on, and everyone has the right to choose their own path.
how: Take on a new kind of project outside your usual field while keeping your main work going, as Sakurai did with his YouTube channel.
anti_pattern: Expecting yourself or other creators to keep doing only what fans want.
example: Sakurai started this YouTube channel while still making games.

title: Competition and Abundance
principle: Keep creating games to deepen your understanding of why games are fun
why: Others will keep creating if you quit, so stay because you want to; Sakurai says making games himself deepened his understanding of why games are fun.
how: Treat each project, even a hobby one, as study of what makes games fun, and remember how much labor sits behind every game you play.
quote: By taking the leap into the field of game creation myself, I’ve gained a deeper understanding and awareness of why games are fun.

title: A World Without Footprints
principle: Study others' games by playing them blind, without spoilers or guides
why: Without preconceptions your impressions are your own, you feel more and you experience every surprise; Sakurai calls this the best way to study someone else's work.
how: Avoid trailers, strategy sites and Let's Plays until you finish, and open a guide only as a last resort when truly stuck.
anti_pattern: Watching Let's Plays or reading guides before forming your own impressions.
quote: In terms of studying someone else's work, there's no better way to do it than this.

title: A World Without Footprints
principle: Form your own verdict before looking up what others think
why: Sakurai wants his impressions to be his alone, without anything else coloring his opinion.
how: Finish the game and settle your own impressions first, then read reviews and community discussion.
anti_pattern: Letting buzz or others' takes shape your view before you have played.
quote: If you want to know what other people think, wait until you're done to look into it.

title: Playing Games in Front of Other People
principle: Imagine presenting your work to customers to uncover insights
why: Thinking up a presentation helps you organize your own thoughts (the teacher becomes the student), and picturing reactions can reveal new insights.
how: Even if you will never present it, mentally walk through showing your game and note how players and customers would react.
quote: Oh, and did you know that thinking up a presentation can help you organize your own thoughts?

title: 1986: The Year of Legend
principle: Study formative eras of games, then carve a new path
why: The path today's creators walk was carved by their predecessors, and knowing it is the basis for creating a new path of your own.
how: Play landmark titles from eras like 1986 (many are playable today) and note which conventions began there before designing your own.
example: 1986: the Famicom Disk System and megabit ROMs expanded game capacity.
quote: And now, we have to do our best to create a new path of our own.

title: Say It, and It Might Come True
principle: Turn negative feelings into concrete questions about how to improve
why: A negative outlook can be a bigger opportunity for change than a positive one if you use it as motivation.
how: When you think 'my work feels pointless,' rewrite it as 'what are some ways I can make it better?' and act on the answer.
anti_pattern: Treating this as forced positivity that denies negative feelings.
quote: If you can use a negative situation as motivation to improve, that might actually be more effective.

title: Say It, and It Might Come True
principle: Stop voicing defeatist thoughts aloud or on social media
why: Each time you think, say or post a negative idea it becomes a little more true, because your thoughts and words set your attitude toward life.
how: Catch yourself before saying or posting lines like 'there's barely any point in working,' and reframe them or drop them.
anti_pattern: Repeating negative ideas out loud or on social media.
quote: What I mean to say is, your thoughts and words establish your attitude toward life!

title: Say It, and It Might Come True
principle: Psych yourself up and act head-on when facing a challenge
why: The words you speak tend to set the course of your actions, and those who act are the ones who win.
how: Before a hard task, tell yourself 'Do it! Come on! Go!' and start immediately.
quote: To tie it back to the power of suggestion, those who act are the ones who win.

title: Storage Tips
principle: Keep reference games and hardware set up for instant access
why: Old games still come in handy for his work, such as footage for the channel, and keeping many systems in one place makes them quick and convenient to use.
how: House consoles together behind a video selector, with switchable power and good ventilation, so you can boot any system in moments.
anti_pattern: Letting the collection go unorganized, which only gets worse over time.
example: Sakurai's custom six-door game cabinet with a selector, used in both his office and his living room.
quote: Especially considering that these old games still come in handy for my line of work.

title: Echo Chambers
principle: Seek out opinions from outside the circle that agrees with you
why: A flood of agreement makes you feel right even though many people disagree, and an insular world makes you lose sight of problems that need solving.
how: When judging design ideas or reviews, check whether you're only seeing approval, and deliberately ask people outside that community.
anti_pattern: Letting in only the opinions that validate you.
quote: You might play things safer, or you may push it further— and in either case, if you can't stay objective, your game will surely end up unbalanced.

title: Echo Chambers
principle: Keep your deliberate unique direction while adapting to team concerns
why: Going in your own "unbalanced" direction can feel best and beats being swayed by others, since a unique vision gives a game distinctive strength, but balance still matters.
how: Listen to and adapt to your team's concerns, but don't sand off the distinctive choices just to please outside voices.
anti_pattern: Being swayed by others until the game loses its identity.
quote: when making games, sometimes taking things in your own "unbalanced" direction is what feels best!

title: The Limitations of Skeletons
principle: Don't let convenient tools set the limits of your ideas
why: If you're too tied to convenient systems, you struggle to step away from them and form mental boundaries about what's possible.
how: Regularly ask which "impossible" ideas are only limits of a tool, and push past them.
anti_pattern: Treating a standard tool's defaults as the boundary of what's possible.
quote: If you're too tied down to convenient systems, you'll end up struggling to step away from their convenience.

title: When Ideas Won't Come
principle: Define the problem's theme before you start generating ideas
why: Thinking of something from nothing leaves no clear starting point, so ideas naturally won't come.
how: Write the problem as a simple one-line theme, e.g., "how to put out a fire in some ruins."
anti_pattern: Brainstorming with no defined problem.
quote: If you try to think of something from nothing, you won't have a clear starting point. And then it'll only be natural if the ideas won't come.

title: When Ideas Won't Come
principle: Generate many solutions first and prune them later
why: Even unrealistic ideas are better than none; quantity gets you past the feeling of having nothing and opens the path to improvements.
how: List broad solution types, including silly ones, and note why each fails in context before cutting any.
anti_pattern: Discarding minor or silly ideas too early.
quote: Quantity over quality— save the pruning for later.

title: When Ideas Won't Come
principle: Mine rejected ideas for variants that fix their flaws
why: Following each thread instead of passing over minor ideas can lead to an answer.
how: For each failed idea, ask what tweak would make it work (no sand, try dirt; bucket too small, try a bigger one).
example: Fire in ruins: sand is hard to find but dirt might work; a bigger bucket might work.

title: Never Get Into Fights
principle: Never fight with or badmouth coworkers; you will meet them again
why: Developers move between teams constantly and the industry is small, so someone you wronged may join your next team years later; treating people poorly gets you excluded.
how: Leave every team on good terms, finish or hand off your work instead of abandoning a project, and don't speak ill of anyone.
anti_pattern: Fighting, acting selfishly, leaving on bad terms, or abandoning a project to dive into the next job.
example: Directors at other companies ask Sakurai about former team members who are interviewing with them.
quote: Unfortunately, the game industry is much smaller than you might think. So, never get into fights!

title: Never Get Into Fights
principle: Raise problems as constructive feedback, then step back rather than resent
why: Speaking your mind often benefits everyone and distancing yourself from a bad fit is fine, but disliking people comes straight back to you.
how: Bring issues up directly and constructively; if a situation still doesn't suit you, distance yourself instead of escalating or holding a grudge.
anti_pattern: Thinking poorly of people.
quote: It's okay to distance yourself from a situation that doesn't suit you. And it's okay to be up-front with constructive feedback.

title: Never Get Into Fights
principle: Put your attention on supportive teammates, not the unpleasant few
why: You're responsible for your workplace's atmosphere, and fixating on difficult people draws attention away from the supportive ones who cause no issues.
how: Engage with the people who help, and keep the team aimed at one common goal.
quote: teams and coworkers should be striving together toward a single, common goal.

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: Finale Special
principle: Favor speed and brevity over perfecting every detail
why: With limited time, over-working each script to prevent every misunderstanding would have cost succinctness; he calls this the secret to a good presentation.
how: Write in fast passes (he averaged about 12 scripts a day) and accept living with the results.
anti_pattern: Ruminating over every last detail.
quote: Short and snappy! Speed above all else! And I'd have to live with the results.
